newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW - Asia should tap business to build - W.Bank.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Asia should tap business to build - W.Bank.

text.p: East Asia's public sector leaders need to think more like private sector executives if the region is to meet its rapidly growing infrastructure needs, a World Bank official said on Monday.

"In future, infrastructure must be treated as a business and not as a public service," Harinder Kohli, World Bank senior operations adviser, East Asia and Pacific Region, told Reuters in an interview.

"There is a need to focus much more on efficiency, cost and quality and not just on quantity. That means governments cannot rely on the public sector alone because it has neither the necessary financial nor managerial resources," he said.
To foster dialogue between government and business, the World Bank is bringing together about 100 public and private sector representatives in Jakarta on September 2-4.

The idea is "to create a dialogue between public and private sector officials to find out why, despite all the promises, the progress made so far in attracting the private sector has been very limited", Kohli said.
East Asia will need to invest US$1.2-US$1.5 trillion in infrastructure over the next decade, World Bank figures show.

Annual investment is expected to rise from some US$75 million now to over US$200 million per year by the early part of next century, Kohli said. These figures suggest that East Asian governments will need to spend 6.5 to seven percent of gross domestic product on infrastructure in coming years compared to five to 5.5 percent now.
"That's not easy to do when governments are also trying to cut deficits and spending," said Kohli.

One of the biggest hurdles in attracting private sector participation in the region's infrastructure has been the wide gap between what government officials think is a fair rate of return on investment and what business is willing to accept.
"If the private sector can be persuaded that the government has done something to reduce the risks it may be willing to accept a lower return," said Kohli.

At the same time, the government sometimes must realise that the rate it is offering is too low, he said. The crucial point, however, is that governments should think not in terms of the return on equity to the project sponsor, but rather in terms of the price the public is paying for the service provided by the project.
"If the private sector is more efficient, it can get a high return on equity while the consumer still gets a lower price," Kohli said.

"Most governments view private sector participation as meaning financing, but in reality, those countries that have been most successful, such as Chile, bring in the private sector to increase efficiency and competitiveness," said Kohli.
Other nagging problems in East Asian countries include slow and opaque government decisions in awarding contracts. Poorly developed legal and regulatory systems also unnerve potential investors.
Assessing risks -- and which parties should bear them -- is another problem for the public and private sectors to thrash out.
Lastly, East Asian countries do not yet have the debt capital markets that could provide the type of long-term financing that infrastructure projects need, Kohli said.
